title: The World on a Brass Ring
story:
James stared in quiet wonder at the massive, spinning sphere. He saw the winding blue threads of painted rivers. He saw the sharp, gilded ridges of distant mountain ranges. He saw the wide, empty stretches of paper oceans where tiny sea monsters were drawn in faded, elegant ink. The world was so much larger than the sun-dappled branches of his youth, larger even than the smoking chimneys of Oakhaven.

With a soft, deliberate motion, this man reached out and placed his palm against the equator of the brass globe, bringing its long journey to a gentle halt. He leaned down, his eyes wrinkling with warmth, and pointed a finger toward a tiny, unlabeled smudge of deep green tucked far away from the sprawling, ink-marked cities. He whispered two words that made James's heart leap: the Great Canopy. 

James reached down to touch the brass canister hanging against his ribs, thinking of the long, dusty path that had brought him here. He had walked the lonely hillside, crossed the Whispering Flats, and ridden the quiet canal, all to find himself standing before a map of everything that ever was. To him, the journey had felt like an eternity, but on this great brass sphere, his entire life was merely a speck of green paint.

Seeing the monkey's intense fascination, Barnaby smiled and reached into a small wooden drawer built into the globe's ornate pedestal. He pulled out a small, circular brass magnifying lens threaded onto a soft green silk ribbon. Leaning down, he gently draped the ribbon around James's neck, offering him a tool to see the smallest secrets of the world. James held the cool lens in his hand, feeling its pleasant weight.

He did not look at the map right away. Instead, James held the glass up to his eye and looked through it at his companion. The gentle lines of this man's face were magnified, warm and clear in the golden glow of the library's chandeliers. In the quiet, dusty air of the rotunda, James felt a profound sense of safety, knowing that no matter how small he was on the map, he was exactly where he belonged.
